free.q: Is it free to get started?
free.a: Yes. You can create an account and track your finances for free, with no credit card required. Upgrade anytime if you need advanced features.

security.a: Your data is encrypted in transit and at rest. We never sell your information to third parties, and you stay in control of what you share.

business.q: Can I use it for my business?
business.a: Yes. Alongside personal budgeting, you can track company spending, manage teams and get financial insights from one place.

mobile.a: Yes. Your account syncs across every device, so your budget is always up to date whether you're on desktop or on the go.

cancel.a: Absolutely. There are no long-term contracts. You can downgrade or cancel your plan whenever you want, no questions asked.

privacy.intro: Your financial data is personal. This Privacy Policy explains what information FinanceApp collects, why we collect it, how we protect it and what rights you have under the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR).

controller.title: 1. Who we are
paragraphs: The data controller is FinanceApp SRL, 10 Exemplu Street, District 1, Bucharest, Romania, Trade Register no. J40/1234/2024, VAT no. RO12345678.
You can reach our Data Protection Officer at dpo@financeapp.com.

dataCollected.title: 2. Data we collect
paragraphs: Account data: name, email address, encrypted password, preferred language and theme.
Profile data you choose to provide: occupation, monthly income, household size and financial goals.
Financial data: transactions, categories, budgets, savings targets and, if you connect a bank, account balances and transaction history.
Payment data: subscription plan and billing history. Card details are handled directly by our payment processor and never stored on our servers.
Technical data: IP address, browser and device type, and usage logs used for security and troubleshooting.

To keep your account secure and prevent fraud (legal basis: legitimate interest).
To send product updates and newsletters, only if you opt in (legal basis: consent, which you can withdraw at any time).

sharing.title: 4. Sharing your data
paragraphs: We never sell your personal or financial data. We share it only with trusted processors that help us run the Service — cloud hosting, payment processing, email delivery and bank connection providers — under data processing agreements.
We may disclose data to public authorities only when required by law.

paragraphs: Your data is stored on servers located in the European Union. If a processor transfers data outside the EEA, we rely on Standard Contractual Clauses approved by the European Commission or other appropriate safeguards.

rule503020.title: The 50/30/20 rule: a simple budget that actually works
rule503020.excerpt: Split your income into needs, wants and savings. Here is how to apply this classic rule to a Romanian salary and adjust it to your life.
body: The 50/30/20 rule is one of the easiest ways to start budgeting: 50% of your net income goes to needs (rent, utilities, groceries, transport), 30% to wants (eating out, hobbies, travel) and 20% to savings and paying off debt.

Start by looking at the last three months of transactions in FinanceApp. Tag each expense as a need or a want and compare the result with the target percentages. Most people are surprised by how much the "wants" category really takes.

The rule is a starting point, not a law. If you live in an expensive city, a 60/20/20 split might be more realistic. What matters is that savings get paid first, automatically, at the beginning of every month.

emergencyFund.title: How to build an emergency fund from zero
emergencyFund.excerpt: Three to six months of expenses sounds like a lot. We break it down into small, realistic steps anyone can follow.
body: An emergency fund protects you from unexpected costs — a car repair, a medical bill or a period without income — without going into debt.
Set a first mini-goal of one month of essential expenses. Create a savings target in FinanceApp and set up an automatic transfer on payday, even if it is only 100 lei.
Keep the money in a separate, easily accessible savings account. Once you hit the first milestone, raise the target to three months, then six.

analytics.title: 5 insights hidden in your spending analytics
analytics.excerpt: Your Analytics page knows more about your habits than you think. Learn how to read trends, category breakdowns and budget health.
body: The trend chart shows how your spending evolves month by month. A slow, steady increase in one category is often more dangerous than a single large purchase.
Check the Budget Health indicator weekly: it compares how much of the month has passed with how much of your budget you have already used.
Finally, look at your top three categories. Reducing just one of them by 10% can free up hundreds of lei every month.

debtFree.title: How Ana paid off 32,000 lei of debt in 18 months
debtFree.excerpt: A nurse from Cluj shares how a clear budget, the snowball method and a lot of patience helped her become debt-free.
body: "I had two credit cards and a personal loan, and I never knew exactly how much I owed," says Ana. The first step was listing every debt in one place.
She used the snowball method: minimum payments on everything, and every extra leu went to the smallest debt. Each closed debt gave her motivation to keep going.
Today Ana has no debt and an emergency fund of four months. "The app did not do the work for me, but it made the progress visible every single day."

impulseShopping.title: The 48-hour rule that stops impulse shopping
impulseShopping.excerpt: Online stores are designed to make you buy fast. A simple waiting rule can save you thousands of lei per year.
body: Before any non-essential purchase over 200 lei, add the item to a wishlist and wait 48 hours. Most of the time the urge simply disappears.
Unsubscribe from promotional emails, remove saved cards from shopping apps and set a monthly "fun money" budget in FinanceApp for guilt-free spending.

freelancer.title: Budgeting as a freelancer: irregular income, stable life
freelancer.excerpt: When income changes every month, a classic budget breaks. Here is a system built for freelancers and PFA owners.
body: Calculate your baseline: the minimum you need each month to cover personal and business expenses. That becomes your "salary".
Every payment you receive goes into a buffer account first. From there, pay yourself the same salary every month and set aside taxes and social contributions separately.
In good months the buffer grows; in slow months it keeps your life stable. Aim for a buffer of at least three months of baseline expenses.

cashFlow.title: Cash flow basics every small business owner should know
cashFlow.excerpt: Profit on paper does not pay the bills. Learn how to forecast cash flow and avoid the most common small business traps.
body: Cash flow is the movement of money in and out of your business. You can be profitable and still run out of cash if clients pay late.
Build a simple 13-week forecast: expected income, fixed costs, variable costs and taxes. Update it every Monday.
Negotiate shorter payment terms with clients, longer ones with suppliers, and keep a cash reserve for at least one month of fixed costs.

inflation.title: Inflation and your savings: what you can do in 2026
inflation.excerpt: Money kept in a current account loses value every year. We compare simple options for protecting your savings.
body: When inflation is higher than the interest you receive, your savings lose purchasing power, even if the number in your account stays the same.
Options such as term deposits, government bonds or diversified index funds can help. Each has a different level of risk and liquidity.
This article is for educational purposes only and is not investment advice. Always consider your goals and, if needed, talk to a licensed advisor.

coupleBudget.title: Mihai & Laura: one budget, zero money fights
coupleBudget.excerpt: A young couple from Bucharest explains how a shared budget helped them save for their first home in just two years.
body: "We used to argue about small things, like who paid for groceries," says Laura. They decided to put all shared expenses into a single budget.
Each keeps a personal allowance, and everything else goes into common categories and one savings goal: the down payment for an apartment.
Two years later, they moved into their first home. "Seeing the goal grow together every month kept us motivated."
